newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo govt promises help to ailing bank industry.
newsitem.headline: Yugo govt promises help to ailing bank industry.

text.p: Yugoslavia's deputy prime minister Danko Djunic promised on Thursday more government help in rehabilitating the ailing banking sector but also called on banks to downsize and adjust to the economy's needs.
"This economy does not need services of so many banks," Djunic said, addressing the annual meeting of the Yugoslav Banking Association (YBA).
According to the latest YBA report, Yugoslavia has 111 banks which together posted a 70 million dinar ($12.15 million) loss in 1996 with unrecoverable claims growing to 3.5 billion dinars.

The government was preparing three major programmes to help ease widespread illiquidity of the entire economy, ease the burden on banks of enormous frozen savings and speed up Yugoslavia's return to international financial community, Djunic said.

The so-called multilateral compensation -- a highly technical inter-company debt settlement scheme -- should be conducted by the end of July under supervision of the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY).
Inter-company debt is estimated at almost $7 billion.
"Part of this debt will remain unsettled (after the operation). Those black holes must also be covered, but the deficit will be much lower," Djunic said.
By law, banks should cover the unsettled debt by extending credits to firms, but in practice they have no lending capacity and would inevitably knock on the NBY's door to borrow.
"That would be disastrous and would lead to a fresh primary issue," a financial analyst said.
Economists did not expect NBY to extend credits to banks but instead saw a possibility of a simple debt forgiveness.
Djordje Djukic, head of the Yugoslav parliament's monetary committee and a member of the NBY Board of Governors, insisted the NBY would provide no credit support for unsettled debt.
Djunic promised bankers that the government would soon finalise a law on releasing more than $4 billion in hard currency savings frozen since 1991.
According to earlier plans, the savings will be recognised as public debt and the state will issue bonds to service it.
Djunic said the federal government had postponed the adoption of the frozen savings programme until Serbia adopted its privatisation law.
Under the federal law, frozen savings holders will be issued bonds, while under the Serbian privatisation law they will be able to use bonds at their face value to buy shares in firms.

"These are only some activities aimed at reconstructing and rehabilitating the banking sector. But it is also needed that the number of banks is reduced in a natural and economically justified way," Djunic said.
The deputy prime minister also said the inflow of foreign funds was closely linked to the presence of more foreign banks.

"These are not only commercial banks but also investment banks and brokerages. They will be attracted by privatisation and further development of our financial market," Djunic said. Borka Vucic, head of Yugoslavia's largest banking group Beogradska Banka Group, said bankers should not be afraid of foreign competition and saw foreign financial institutions bringing modern management standards and know-how.
-- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
($1 = 5.7615 Yugoslav dinars)
